hints: The motion consists of three consecutive phases: constant acceleration from rest, constant velocity at $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and constant deceleration to rest.
On a velocity-time graph, this forms a trapezium with straight line segments.
Since deceleration magnitude is twice the acceleration magnitude, the downward-sloping segment on the right must be twice as steep as the upward-sloping segment on the left.
walkthrough: Understand the features of a velocity-time graph: constant acceleration is represented by straight lines, where gradient equals acceleration.
Draw the acceleration phase: start at $(0, 0)$ and draw a straight line rising to $v = 25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at time $t = T\text{ s}$.
Draw the constant-speed phase: from $t = T$, draw a horizontal line at height $v = 25\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Draw the deceleration phase: draw a downward straight line to the time axis at total time $180\text{ s}$. Because the magnitude of deceleration is double the acceleration, the downward gradient has double the slope magnitude, taking half the duration of the acceleration phase.

hints: The acceleration phase changes speed by $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in time $T$, so acceleration is $a = \frac{25}{T}$.
Deceleration has twice this magnitude, so $d = 2a = \frac{50}{T}$.
The deceleration phase reduces speed by $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so its time is $t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{25}{d} = \frac{25}{50/T} = 0.5T$.
Subtract the acceleration time $T$ and deceleration time $0.5T$ from the total time $180\text{ s}$ to find the constant-speed duration.
walkthrough:
Relate speed change and acceleration: during the initial phase, the train accelerates from rest to $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in time $T$. Hence:
$$\text{Acceleration } a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{25}{T}$$

The problem states that the deceleration has magnitude $2a$:
$$\text{Deceleration } d = 2 \times \left(\frac{25}{T}\right) = \frac{50}{T}$$

During the deceleration phase, the speed drops from $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$ back to $0$:
$$t_{\text{dec}} = \frac{\Delta v}{d} = \frac{25}{50/T} = \frac{25T}{50} = 0.5T\text{ s}$$

Calculate the duration of the constant-speed stage by subtracting the two accelerating and decelerating times from the total time $180\text{ s}$:
$$t_{\text{constant}} = 180 - t_{\text{acc}} - t_{\text{dec}} = 180 - T - 0.5T = 180 - 1.5T\text{ s}$$

hints: The total distance travelled is represented by the area under the velocity-time graph (a trapezium).
Use the trapezium area formula: $\text{Area} = \frac{1}{2}(b_1 + b_2)h$, where bottom base is $180$, top base is $(180 - 1.5T)$, and height is $25$.
Once $T = 64\text{ s}$ is found, calculate the deceleration distance as the area of the deceleration triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times 0.5T \times 25$.
walkthrough: Recall the fundamental property of velocity-time graphs: the distance travelled equals the area under the curve. Here, the graph is a trapezium.

Write the trapezium area formula:
$$\text{Distance} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$$

Substitute the two parallel sides (bottom base $180\text{ s}$ and top base $180 - 1.5T\text{ s}$) and height $25\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$3300 = \frac{1}{2}\left(180 + (180 - 1.5T)\right) \times 25$$
$$3300 = \frac{25}{2}(360 - 1.5T) = 12.5(360 - 1.5T)$$

Compute the time spent decelerating using $t_{\text{dec}} = 0.5T$ from part (ii):
$$t_{\text{dec}} = 0.5 \times 64 = 32\text{ s}$$

Calculate the distance travelled during deceleration as the triangular area under that section:
$$\text{Deceleration Distance} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height} = \frac{1}{2} \times 32 \times 25 = 16 \times 25 = 400\text{ m}$$
